lines.note: Ta completes acrecen-ta from f0483; tsugi wo suru means mending. The parenthesis and temẽte at the far right are displaced type completing conſequẽ- on the following physical row; they remain here rather than being silently reordered.
Tsugi and tsugini mean next or afterwards. The worn initial retains the crossbar of T. The Portuguese doubled-s sort in ißo is visible; conſequẽ- continues in the preceding row’s far-right temẽte.
Tsugina and tsugino qualify the thing that follows. The second form contains gu, not the draft’s ga; the two alternatives express the same following or next relation.
The Portuguese adds that the object is immediately after another. The close printed estàlogo is retained without modernizing its spelling or imposing a new word boundary.
Tsugitsugini is the adverb one after another. Adu. and the Portuguese explanation are italic, and the final de governs outro on the next row.
Outro completes the preceding de; the alternative explanation is after this and that. The line belongs to the successive-order adverb rather than beginning another entry.
Tsugi, tsugu, tsuida supplies the verb for adding or joining. The principal parts preserve the historical inflection, and the italic definition continues with things of the same kind.

The example lists water and a second liquid, interpreted as sake from the following vinho and the later ſaqe example. Enlarged type here still favours printed taqe, a probable damaged or anomalous initial; that visible reading is retained rather than silently normalized.
Abura nado wo tsugu completes the example: add oil and similar liquids. The Portuguese starts by translating the water item; agoa retains its historical spelling.

runs.text: vinho, azeite, &c. ou ir ceuando eſtas cou-

lines.note: Wine and oil complete the list, followed by the sense of continually feeding or replenishing these substances. Cou- visibly divides cousas across the row boundary.
Sas completes cousas. Yo wo hi ni tsugu joins night to day: continuing an effort urgently. Apreſarſe is retained with the printed consonant sequence rather than expanded to modern apressar-se.

runs.text: muito ajuntando as noites aos dias. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese explains extreme haste by joining nights to days. Iqi- begins the next Japanese expression, iki wo tsugu, with a visible line-end hyphen.
Uo tsugu completes iki wo tsugu, to take breath and rest. The Portuguese confirms respiration here rather than the general adding or succession sense of the headword.

Inochi wo, alternatively kubi wo tsugu, is glossed as living or continuing alive. The punctuation after Inochiuo and the Latin alternative marker are preserved rather than converted into a continuous modern Japanese sentence.

runs.text: ou continuar com a vida. ¶ Item,

lines.note: The first gloss concludes with continuing in life. Item opens a distinct causative or rescuing use of the same expression, beginning Ino- across the physical break.
Ino- plus chiuo forms inochi wo tsugu; kubi wo tsugu again supplies an alternative. Dar a vi- begins the explanation of granting or saving someone’s life, distinct from merely remaining alive above.

runs.text: da a alguem que eſtaua pera ſer morto, ou juſti-

lines.note: Da completes vida: the beneficiary had been about to be killed or executed. The final juſti- has a visible terminal division mark and continues as -çado below.
Çado completes the execution gloss. Ki wo tsugu introduces grafting a tree, directly translated by enxertar; the capital Q is part of the ordinary qe/qi spelling system.
Sao wo tsugu means lengthening a pole by joining another section. The Portuguese first names a cane; the printed Sauouo spelling and the tilde in hũa are preserved.

runs.text: ou vara a outra pera abrãger, ou chegar mais.

lines.note: A second rod is added to the first so it can reach farther. Abrãger retains its abbreviation tilde rather than being expanded to a modern spelling.
Mizutsugi is a vessel used to pour or add water. The compound belongs to the liquid-replenishing sense of tsugu, and its explanation continues below.
The water-vessel definition ends here, followed by abura tsugi, an oil-pouring vessel. The visible word separation in Abura tçugui is retained, contrasting with the closed compound above.

runs.text: Vaſo com que deitão azeite, ou ceuão a cãdea.

lines.note: This vessel pours oil or feeds the lamp. Enlarging the final noun reveals the weak nasal mark and a damaged a in cãdea, replacing OCR cqdea; the abbreviation is preserved without supplying the omitted n.
Yo wo tsugu describes succession to rule or to an inherited estate. The Portuguese Soceder spelling is retained; its alternative object follows on the next physical line.
Mòrgado completes the inherited-estate sense. Ato wo tsugu then means inheriting the house or succeeding to someone’s position; the printed Erdar and close acaſa are retained.

runs.text: ou ſoceder no lugar dalgũ ſuperior, ou meſtre,

lines.note: The successor takes the place of a superior or master. Dalgũ retains the abbreviated nasal ending, and the list continues with &c. rather than stopping at this line.

Kubisu wo tsugu evokes people close behind one another, literally joining heels. The scan supports the object particle uo in Cubiſuuo, not OCR no; the Portuguese describes many people gathered together.

Sode wo tsurane, kubisu wo tsugu describes sleeves in a line and heels following closely. The b and uo in the repeated cubiſuuo correct the malformed cuǒiſuuo reading; Idẽ refers back to the crowded gathering.

runs.text: Parte, ou juntura onde ſe conti-

lines.note: Tsugime is a joint or joining place. The Portuguese begins the relative clause describing where one object is continued, with conti- divided at the visible terminal mark.

runs.text: nua a couſa, ou ajunta, & gruda com outra.

lines.note: Nua completes continua. The remaining explanation specifies joining and adhering to another object, so the entry concerns a physical seam or junction rather than temporal succession.
Tsugimono names something added or joined. Its Portuguese description continues with an attached or united object, subsequently illustrated by repaired pottery.

runs.text: & vnida com outra, como porſolana, ou vaſo

lines.note: The object is united with another, for example porcelain or a vessel. Porſolana is preserved as printed, without substituting a modern Portuguese spelling for porcelain.

runs.text: com algũa parte pegada, que ſe quebrou.

lines.note: The vessel has a broken part attached again. This completes the concrete explanation of tsugimono as a joined or repaired object rather than an abstract addition.
Tsugiki is a graft or grafted tree, matching both Portuguese alternatives. The damaged initial retains the capital T’s upper bar and height, so the draft’s lowercase t is corrected.
Tsugisoye, tsugisoyuru, tsugisoyeta denotes replenishing or adding further. The historical y spelling and principal parts are preserved; the Portuguese acre- continues below.
Centando completes acrecentando, with oil and wine illustrating replenishment. The italic Vt introduces a Japanese example whose initial A- begins abura across the physical line break.
A- plus bura forms abura; the example means replenishing oil, sake, and the like. This row clearly prints hooked long ſ in ſaqe, providing a local comparison for the anomalous taqe in c1-l008.

runs.text: Summa de toda a conta, ou aſomando

lines.note: Tsugoo is the total or sum of an account. The caron over o is visible and is retained; the Portuguese then gives the operation of adding everything together.
The definition concludes with all items summed. Tsugoo wa ikahodo zo asks how much the total is; the repeated caron agrees with the headword, and Em begins the translation.
Em summa is completed here: what is it in total, or after adding? The printed aſomando remains a historical accounting expression rather than being replaced by a modern synonym.
Tsugomori and the metathesized variant tsumogori name the last day of the month. Both printed forms are retained; their lexical relationship does not authorize regularizing the second to the first.
Dia domes completes derradeiro: the month’s last day. The close domes is preserved as printed, and the short continuation remains a separate body row.
Tsugumi is described as a bird like a thrush. The gloss provides the comparison directly; the doubled-s sort in paßaro is retained without changing the printed orthography.

runs.text: Hũa aue de rapina como minhoto que

lines.note: Tsuguri here names a bird of prey, compared with minhoto. The historical bird-name is retained; the scan and brief gloss do not require a more precise modern species identification.
The bird eats small creatures, snakes, and the like. This relative clause completes the preceding bird-of-prey entry and is unrelated to the following homographic thread-ball noun.

runs.text: Nouelo de linhas, retros, ou outro fio.

lines.note: The second tsuguri is a ball of thread, silk twist, or another fibre. The distinct Portuguese definition establishes a separate homographic entry despite the repeated headword.
Tsuguri ni suru means winding into a ball, translated by ennouelar. The complete example closes the column; there is no lost continuation or catchword at its lower edge.

runs.text: Palaura que jũta aos verbos denota preſ-

lines.note: Tsui is an element prefixed to verbs to express haste or added force. The scan shows jũta with a tilde over u, correcting jãta; preſ- begins the divided Portuguese noun for haste.

runs.text: ſa, ou algũa energia, & vigor, & às vezes

lines.note: The element can convey energy and vigour as well as haste. The final às vezes introduces the alternative stylistic function described on the following row.
Sometimes the prefix adds no more than elegance. Tsui kaku is the first example, writing quickly or readily; the abbreviated q̃ and the printed no remain unexpanded.
Creuer completes Eſ-creuer, writing quickly or easily. Tçuimo- starts tsuimodoru, the next prefixed verb, across the physical line break.
Doru completes tsuimodoru, to return quickly. Tsuihatasu then introduces finishing something promptly; the final punctuation appears as the printed comma and is retained as such.
The Portuguese translates tsuihatasu as finishing something quickly. Enlargement supports depreßa without the draft’s intrusive i; the short row completes the prefix entry.

runs.text: Couſa ſemelhante, ou correſpõdãte a outra.

lines.note: This separate tsui entry concerns resemblance or correspondence, hence a matching pair. The printed abbreviated correſpõdãte is retained with its two nasal marks rather than regularized from the following example.
Kore wa tsui ja means that this is a matching counterpart. The translation says it is of the same kind; meſmala- keeps the close setting before the divided laya.
Ya completes laya, kind or class. Tçui suru introduces matching or corresponding to another thing; the scan has contiguous correſpondẽte, without the OCR’s internal space.

runs.text: drar hũa couſa com outra, ou correſpõder.

lines.note: Drar completes quadrar: one thing fits or corresponds to another. The abbreviated nasal in correſpõder is distinct from the preceding row’s spelling and is preserved.
Tsuiku denotes a matched pair of verses. The definition emphasizes their resemblance and continues by describing their dependence on each other.
The paired verses depend on one another. Bin itsui then supplies a practical counting example, a pair of vessels; the single printed t in itçui is retained.
Bin itsui is translated as a pair of bules, small vessels. Fude ittsui then gives a pair of writing implements; the doubled tt differs visibly from the preceding example’s itçui.
Par de penas completes Hum, a pair of pens. This is the Portuguese explanation of fude ittsui rather than another entry or a missing section heading.

runs.text: Caſtigo, ou morte, ou iuſtiça por al-

lines.note: Tsuibat denotes punishment, death, or judicial execution for an offence. The Japanese final t is the historical checked coda and should not be expanded to tçu; Portuguese al- continues below.
Gum completes algum maleficio, some wrongdoing. Tsuibat suru is the verbal example, imposing that punishment; the damaged initial retains a capital T rather than OCR l.

runs.text: Supplemento que ſe faz pera ſuprir o

lines.note: Tsuika is an addition or supplement made to supply a deficiency. The following row limits the explanation to missing material in a book or written text.

runs.text: que faltou em algum liuro, ou eſcritura.

lines.note: The supplement supplies what was absent from a book or document. Liuro and eſcritura retain their printed historical letterforms, and the complete clause closes the entry.

runs.text: Certo modo de ſebe, parede, ou vallo.

lines.note: Tsuikaki names a kind of fence, wall, or enclosure. The visible capital T supplies the initial omitted by the draft; the alternatives describe the structure without identifying one modern construction material.

Tsuikoo is explained by carving or relief on trays and incense boxes. The headword has a circumflex, while cǒbaco has a caron; the distinction follows the two visible marks, not a normalized pronunciation.

runs.text: tos releuos, ou molduras, & lauores com va-

lines.note: Tos completes certos: certain reliefs, mouldings, and decorative work. Va- begins varias, whose colours are described on the following physical row.

runs.text: rias tintas dalguãs peças de pao acharoado q̃

lines.note: The decoration uses various colours on lacquered wooden pieces. Enlargement shows a broken wavy tilde over the final a in dalguãs, replacing the draft’s grave; the q̃ abbreviation is left unexpanded.
The pieces come from China. Tsuikoo no mono means an object of this workmanship; its visible circumflex corrects the draft’s caron. O- begins Portuguese obra on the next row.
Bra completes obra: work of this form or decorative technique. This finishes the example and does not supply another Japanese synonym.

Tsuiku refers the reader back to tsui, where the paired-verse sense has already been explained. Enlargement supports the unusual italic final i in the referenced word; this mixed typeface is preserved rather than made uniform.

Tsuide is an occasion or turn. Tsuide wo motte begins an example of going when an opportunity presents itself. The V of Vt is damaged; its surviving form is provisionally read with the italic t and the nearby italic Vt examples.
Mairoo completes the intention to go when convenient. The dotted final i in Irei corrects OCR Ires and agrees with the Japanese prospective form; auẽdo retains its abbreviation tilde.
Tsuide gatera means in passing or while taking this opportunity. The r in gatera is visible, correcting gateta; the construction expresses doing something alongside the main purpose.
Ocaſião completes com eſta ocaſião, with this opportunity. The short continuation closes tsuide gatera and remains a separate physical row.

Tsuideni has the same adverbial sense. The example is te no tsuide ni. Separate reinspection of the high terminal and faint rounded bowl supports a heavily abraded d in tçuide-, compared with nearby Tçuide; this chosen restoration remains a nonblocking reading caveat.
Ni completes the occasion phrase, followed by kore wo shite kudasarei, please do this. The polite request is translated as taking advantage of the addressee already being occupied with the task.

runs.text: amão na maßa, peçouos que façais iſto.

lines.note: The Portuguese idiom says that, since the hand is already in the dough, please do this as well. Enlargement identifies the doubled-s sort in maßa, correcting OCR maia; the printed close amão and peçouos remain.

Tsuifami describes a bird picking up food. The historical principal-part abbreviations u and ǒda are retained without imposing a modern inflection; the Portuguese object and agent continue on the next row.

runs.text: paßaro ogrão, ou comer com o bico.

lines.note: The bird takes the grain, or eats with its beak. This supplies the pecking sense of tsuifami; the doubled-s sort in paßaro and close ogrão are retained as printed.
Tsuihoo, explained by oi hanasu, means expelling someone from the land. The headword has f rather than OCR r, and terra has two r types; the caron is preserved.
The gloss restates exile or banishment. Tsuihoo no quan- begins the designation of officials charged with expulsion; the printed quan- continues as -nin on the next physical row.

runs.text: Homens que tem por officio deſterrar,

lines.note: Nin completes quannin, officials. Their stated office is to carry out banishment, matching the preceding tsuihoo example; the Portuguese sentence continues below.
The officials expel people from the land. This closes the banishment entry before the separate property-confiscation term begins.

runs.text: Caſtigo, ou pena de tomar a alguẽ

lines.note: Tsuifuku denotes punishment by confiscating someone’s property. The clear headword f and the following gloss establish this reading; the attributed NINJAL entry independently agrees on the lexical form.
The estate and goods are taken as forfeited. Tçui- begins a longer illustrative sentence about the officials who perform this confiscation.

runs.text: fucuno quãninga maitte xizai zǒguuo v-

lines.note: Tsuifuku no quannin ga maitte begins the officials’ arrival and seizure of private possessions. The initial f has lost its upper hook and its remnant resembles r; the surviving bar, repeated form, and clear headword support fucuno, retained with this caveat. The scan also supports abbreviated quãninga and the final v- beginning ubai.

Bai totta completes ubai totta, seized and took away. Feiq. is the Heike citation label and Lib. 1 its book reference; Vindo os starts the Portuguese account. The draft’s extra g before os has no corresponding letter.

runs.text: officiais do fiſco, & tomando toda a riqueza,

lines.note: The fiscal officers come and take all the wealth. The initial of riqueza is r, not the draft’s x; the clause continues with movable property below.

Mouel completes the description of confiscated possessions. Shizai wo tsuifuku suru means confiscating private property; the damaged f has a surviving crossbar and upper stub, supporting f rather than OCR r. To- begins the Portuguese infinitive.
Mar completes tomar: take the property as forfeited. This restates the confiscation sense and closes the long entry.
Tsuiji is an earthen wall, directly glossed as taipa or parede de barro. The gi spelling belongs to the historical transcription and is not changed to match modern ji.

Tsuini means at last or finally. The worn headword’s surviving T, cedilla, and minims, checked against the attributed NINJAL entry, support Tçuini rather than Fiuiui. Finalmẽte preserves the nasal abbreviation, with its m abraded; the lower Tçui- is a separate catchword.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The catchword anticipates Tçuiqiacu at the opening of f0485.
